bodyHtml:
Best translation software: free tools and professional options

January 3, 2020
Translation tools | Human translation | Machine Translation

Translation software falls into two groups. Machine translation tools turn text from one language into another in seconds, and computer-assisted translation (CAT) tools help professional translators work faster and more consistently. This post covers both, so you can choose the right tool for your task.

Free tools are useful for understanding a message or a menu. They are not designed to take responsibility for a contract, a medical leaflet or your brand voice, and knowing where that line sits will save you time and money.

Free machine translation tools worth knowing

Most people start with a free online translator. These are the tools you are most likely to meet, and what each does well.

Google Translate

Google Translate is the most widely used translation tool. Google added 110 languages in June 2024, its largest expansion to date, which took the total to more than 240.

It handles text, web pages, documents, photos and speech, and you can download languages for offline use when you travel. It is a quick way to get the gist of a text, but it still misses nuance, tone and cultural references.

Microsoft Translator

Microsoft Translator is built into Microsoft products and available as a mobile app. It supports live conversations between several people, which makes it handy for informal chats and travel.

Developers and businesses can also use the Microsoft translation service inside their own apps, which is one reason it appears in so many tools you use every day.

DeepL

DeepL translates text and documents, and its paid plans include glossaries so you can set how key terms are translated. Many people use it for emails and drafts because the wording often reads smoothly. Smooth is not the same as correct, so a fluent sentence can still contain an error.

Reverso and Linguee

Reverso and Linguee work more like bilingual dictionaries than translators. They show your word or phrase in real sentences, which helps you check how a term is used in context.

They are especially useful if you already speak the language and want to confirm a choice. For a longer text, they are a support tool, not a replacement for a translator.

How to get better results from a free translator

A few habits improve machine translation output, whichever tool you use. They cost nothing and reduce the chance of an embarrassing mistake.

  • Write short, plain sentences in the source language, and avoid idioms, slang and wordplay
  • Check names, numbers, dates and units by hand, because these are easy to get wrong and costly when they are
  • Compare the result with a second tool or a bilingual dictionary if a sentence looks odd
  • Ask a native speaker to read anything that customers, partners or the public will see
  • Keep the original text next to the translation so you can trace any problem

Even then, remember that a translation can read well and still be wrong. Fluent output hides errors, which is why review matters.

Software that professional translators use

When you search for "tools for translators", you are usually looking for CAT tools. These platforms do not translate for the linguist. They organise the work so a human translator is faster and more consistent.

The main features are:

  • Translation memory, which stores approved translations and suggests them when the same or similar sentence appears again
  • Termbases and glossaries, which keep product names and key terms consistent
  • Quality checks, which flag missing numbers, inconsistent terms and formatting errors
  • Support for many file types, so the translated file keeps the layout of the original
  • Optional machine translation suggestions, which the translator edits rather than accepts

Well-known CAT tools include Trados Studio, memoQ, Phrase and the free, open-source OmegaT. Software and app teams often use localisation platforms that connect to their code repositories and manage translations alongside releases.

Website owners have similar options. Plugins can machine translate a whole site automatically, but the result often misses the words local customers search for and the tone they expect. Having a native linguist review key pages, or translating your website professionally, protects both your brand and your search visibility.

Translation memory pays off over time. If you publish updated manuals or product pages every year, a translator who uses a memory does not need to retranslate the sentences that have not changed, and your terminology stays stable.

When free translation tools are enough

Free tools are a sensible choice for low-risk tasks, such as:

  • Reading a foreign-language web page or email to understand the main point
  • Checking a word, menu or street sign while travelling
  • Drafting an informal message that a native speaker will check
  • Getting a first impression of a document to decide whether it needs professional translation

When you need a professional translator instead

The risk grows when other people will rely on the text. Contracts, financial statements, product instructions, marketing copy, patient information and anything you plan to publish need a human translator who works into their native language and takes responsibility for the result.

Healthwatch advises that online tools such as Google Translate should not be relied on for translation in healthcare settings, because they can produce inaccurate or misleading communication. The same caution applies to legal and financial documents, where a wrong figure or term has consequences. If a UK court, a Home Office department or a bank asks for a certified translation, a raw machine translation is unlikely to be accepted, and you will need a translator who can certify their work.

Confidentiality is another factor. Before you paste personal or commercially sensitive text into a free tool, check the provider's data terms, because UK GDPR still applies to the information you share.

Machine translation with human review

There is a middle route. Some projects use machine translation as a first draft and a professional linguist then edits it, a process known as post-editing. It can suit large volumes of low-risk content, such as internal knowledge bases or product support articles, where you need speed and a consistent standard.

It is less suitable for creative or persuasive text, such as advertising and brand copy, where the translator needs room to adapt tone and imagery. Ask any agency how it uses machine translation and who checks the final text before you agree to a method.

Cost matters too. Post-editing can be cheaper than translating from scratch, but only when the machine draft is good enough to edit. For a short, high-stakes document, a full human translation is often quicker and safer than repairing a poor draft.

How to choose the right translation tool or service

Start with the purpose of the text and the cost of a mistake. These questions help you decide:

  • Who will read the translation, and will they act on it?
  • Does the text include legal, medical, technical or financial content?
  • Do you need a certified or sworn translation?
  • Is the content confidential or personal?
  • Will you translate the same material repeatedly, so that a translation memory saves money?

If you answer yes to any of these, a human translator is the safer choice. For a language-specific need, such as a reliable Spanish translator, BeTranslated's Spanish team works with native linguists, and other languages are listed on the languages page.

Frequently asked questions

What is the best translation software for beginners?

Google Translate, Microsoft Translator and DeepL are the most common starting points, because they are free to try and easy to use. They work best for short, informal text where a small error will not cause harm.

What software do professional translators use?

Most professionals use CAT tools such as Trados Studio, memoQ, Phrase or OmegaT. These tools store translation memories and glossaries, check quality and handle many file formats, while the translator still does the translating.

Is machine translation accurate enough for business documents?

It can be accurate enough for an internal summary, but it is risky for contracts, regulated content and published material. A human translator can check meaning, terminology and tone, and certify the result when a UK authority requires it.

What is a translation memory?

A translation memory is a database of sentences that have already been translated and approved. When the same or a similar sentence appears again, the tool suggests the stored translation, which saves time and keeps your wording consistent.

Can I use free translation tools for confidential documents?

You should check the provider's data terms first, because free web tools may store or process what you enter. For confidential or personal data, a professional agency with clear confidentiality terms is the safer option.
